<reason>Both sides argued competently, but B built the more durable analytic framework. B's key structural move—distinguishing gambling (transactional, operator-controlled) from pornography (content-based, freely displaceable via links/reposts)—directly answered A's attempted "gotcha" about conceding gambling gating, and A's closing never substantively re-engaged that control/transaction distinction, instead pivoting to accuse B of an inconsistent burden ("demands proof, offers none"), which B's closing correctly flagged as a mischaracterization of its actual proportionality standard. B also sharpened the harm categorization (exclusion from lawful access vs. mere "intrusiveness" the motion already concedes), which meaningfully contested A's attempt to fold all adult costs into the resolution's "even if" clause. A's core analogies (alcohol, cigarettes, liquor cabinets) were physical-goods analogies that B effectively undercut by pointing out digital content's near-zero substitution cost (a link or repost vs. smuggling), and A never fully repaired that disanalogy. A had strong rhetorical framing and organization, and its opening's clipping for exceeding word limit is a real execution cost. Overall B answered pressure more precisely, kept tighter epistemic discipline, and left the debate easier to decide in its favor.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's Rebuttal 1/2 point that digital pornography can be re-linked or reposted without the "smuggling" costs of physical goods like alcohol, which undermined A's central analogy and was never adequately repaired in A's later speeches.</best_rebuttal>
